s: Who can be a whistleblower under the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014?
o: only a Member of Parliament making a complaint to the Lokpal
only a government employee of the Union Government
a public servant or another person, including an NGO, making a public interest disclosure
x: A whistleblower includes any public servant or other person, including an NGO, who makes a public interest disclosure of specified wrongdoing to the Competent Authority.

s: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of the protection available under the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014?
o: Acceptance of anonymous complaints as a general rule
Punishment for knowingly false or frivolous complaints
x: Anonymous complaints are not accepted as a general rule. The complainant’s identity is disclosed to the competent authority but is required to be kept confidential; protection against victimisation is also provided.

s: Under the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, which pair of person complained against and competent authority is correctly matched?
x: For Union Ministers the competent authority is the Prime Minister. Central employees go to the CVC, State Ministers to the CM, and MPs to the Rajya Sabha Chairman or Lok Sabha Speaker.

s: What is the punishment for a knowingly false complaint under the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014?
x: A knowingly false complaint attracts up to 2 years and ₹30,000; revealing a complainant's identity attracts up to 3 years and ₹50,000.

s: Which of the following categories is specifically excluded from the stated whistleblower rules?
x: The Special Protection Group (SPG) is excluded from the stated rules.

s: With the dissolution of which Lok Sabha did the Whistle Blowers Protection (Amendment) Bill, 2015 lapse?
x: The Bill would have barred disclosures in Section 8(1)-type categories; it lapsed with the 16th Lok Sabha in 2019.

s: Within how many years must a complaint under the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 be made?
x: Complaints must be made within 7 years, and anonymous complaints are not entertained.

s: Under the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014, who is the competent authority for a complaint against a Union Minister?
x: Complaints against a Union Minister go to the Prime Minister; against a State Minister to the Chief Minister.

s: Under the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014, what is the punishment for revealing the identity of a complainant?
x: Revealing identity is punishable with up to 3 years and ₹50,000; a false complaint with up to 2 years and ₹30,000.

s: Under the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014, who is the competent authority for complaints against Central Government employees?
x: For Central employees the competent authority is the CVC; for Union Ministers it is the Prime Minister.

s: What did the Whistle Blowers Protection (Amendment) Bill, 2015 seek to do?
o: Bar disclosures in categories like those of RTI Section 8(1), such as security and Cabinet papers
Make the Lokpal the only competent authority
Extend the complaint limit to 10 years
x: The 2015 Bill, passed by the Lok Sabha in May 2015, would bar disclosures in RTI Section 8(1)-type categories; it lapsed in 2019.

s: On which subject was the Santhanam Committee constituted?
x: The Santhanam Committee was the Committee on Prevention of Corruption; the CBI followed in 1963 and the CVC in 1964.

s: The Enforcement Directorate functions primarily under which combination of laws?
o: RTI Act, 2005 and Official Secrets Act, 1923
x: The Enforcement Directorate operates under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, and the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999.

s: The Santhanam Committee led to the setting up of which two bodies?
x: The Santhanam Committee (1962-64) led to the CBI in 1963 and the CVC in 1964.

s: Before the CBI can investigate a case within a State's territory, it needs the consent of that State government under which provision?
o: Section 6 of the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946
Section 17A of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
Section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
Section 8 of the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003
x: The CBI draws its powers from the DSPE Act, 1946, and Section 6 of that Act requires the State's consent. Section 17A PCA is government approval before investigating a public servant's official decisions; Section 19 PCA is sanction before a court takes cognizance; the CVC Act is about the CVC's superintendence, not State consent.

s: Who among the following form the selection committee for the Director of the CBI?
o: Prime Minister, Chief Justice of India or nominee, and Leader of Opposition
President, Vice-President and Speaker of the Lok Sabha
Prime Minister, Union Home Minister and Chief Ministers of all States
Chief Justice of India, Attorney General and Cabinet Secretary
x: The Director of the CBI is chosen by a committee comprising the Prime Minister, the Chief Justice of India or the Chief Justice’s nominee, and the Leader of Opposition.

s: What is the legal status of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)?
o: Non-constitutional, non-statutory body linked to the DSPE Act, 1946
Statutory body under the CVC Act, 2003
Judicial body under the Ministry of Law
x: The CBI is a non-constitutional, non-statutory body whose legal basis is linked to the DSPE Act, 1946.

s: What is the legal status of the Central Vigilance Commission?
o: Department of the Ministry of Finance under the PMLA
Independent statutory body established under the CVC Act, 2003
x: The CVC is an independent statutory body established under the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003.

s: Which body exercises superintendence over the CBI in corruption cases?
x: The CVC supervises the CBI in corruption cases; the CBI rests on the DSPE Act, 1946, and the ED on the PMLA and FEMA.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Central Vigilance Commission?
o: It is a statutory body under the CVC Act 2003
It has superintendence over the CBI in corruption cases
It has up to 2 Vigilance Commissioners
Its members hold office for 5 years or until 65
x: CVC members hold office for 4 years or until 65, not 5 years; the other statements are correct.

s: The Enforcement Directorate functions under which ministry?
x: The ED works under the Ministry of Finance, the CBI under the Ministry of Personnel.

s: Under which ministry does the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) function?
o: Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions
x: The CBI, based on the DSPE Act 1946, works under the Ministry of Personnel.

s: According to the CVC report of September 2026, what was the CBI's conviction rate in 2025?
x: The CVC report put the CBI's conviction rate at 71.71% in 2025, with 7,229 cases pending.

s: In the Andhra Pradesh Lokayukta framework, the Lokayukta primarily deals with:
o: International relations, while the Upa-Lokayukta deals with public order
Only judicial officers, while the Upa-Lokayukta deals with private citizens
Higher functionaries, while the Upa-Lokayukta deals with the rest
Only Group C and D employees, while the Upa-Lokayukta deals with Ministers
x: The Lokayukta has jurisdiction over higher functionaries, whereas the Upa-Lokayukta deals with the remaining categories covered by the state law.

s: Within what period did the 2013 central law on Lokpal and Lokayuktas require every State to set up a Lokayukta?
x: The 2013 Act obliged every State to establish a Lokayukta within one year of its commencement; States then framed widely differing laws. Six months, two years and five years are not the stated period.

s: Who was the first Lokpal of India?
x: Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose became the first Lokpal in March 2019; Justice A.M. Khanwilkar became chairperson in February 2024.

s: Besides the Chairperson, the Lokpal under the 2013 Act may have up to how many members?
x: The Lokpal has a Chairperson and up to 8 members, 50% of them judicial.

s: Which of the following is NOT a member of the Lokpal selection committee?
x: The committee is the PM (chair), Speaker, LoP, CJI or a nominated SC judge and an eminent jurist; the Cabinet Secretary is not on it.

s: In which year was the AP Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta Act, under which Andhra Pradesh's Lokayukta is established, enacted?
x: The AP Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta Act dates from 1983; the Lokayukta deals with higher functionaries.

s: Under the 2024 amendment, who chairs the selection committee that recommends the AP Lokayukta?
o: Chief Justice of the High Court
x: Since the 2024 amendment, a retired HC Chief Justice or Judge is appointed on the recommendation of a committee chaired by the CM, for 5 years.

s: Who became the chairperson of the Lokpal in February 2024?
x: Justice A.M. Khanwilkar became Lokpal chairperson in February 2024; the first Lokpal was Justice P.C. Ghose (2019).

s: Who was sworn in as the Lokayukta of Andhra Pradesh on 25 August 2026?
x: Justice T. Mallikarjuna Rao took oath as AP Lokayukta before Governor S. Abdul Nazeer on 25 August 2026.

s: What share of the members of the Lokpal must be judicial members?
x: Under the 2013 Act, 50% of Lokpal members must be judicial members.

s: Under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, at least half of the Lokpal members must come from which groups?
o: SC, ST, OBC, minorities and women
x: At least 50% of Lokpal members must be from SC, ST, OBC, minorities and women; 50% must be judicial.

s: Under the 2024 amendment, what is the term of the Andhra Pradesh Lokayukta?
x: The 2024 amendment made a retired HC Chief Justice or Judge the Lokayukta, chosen by a CM-led committee, for 5 years.

s: Who pioneered Citizen Report Cards in Bengaluru in the 1990s?
o: Central Vigilance Commission associated with K. Santhanam
Public Affairs Centre associated with Samuel Paul
Planning Commission associated with B. R. Ambedkar
Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan associated with Aruna Roy
x: Citizen Report Cards were developed by the Public Affairs Centre in Bengaluru in the 1990s under the leadership of Samuel Paul.

s: With which of the following is Jan Sunwai, as a method of citizen oversight, most closely associated?
o: Lokpal inquiries in Maharashtra during the 2000s
CVC hearings in Delhi during the 1980s
MKSS public hearings in Rajasthan during the 1990s
SSAAT audits in Andhra Pradesh during the 1970s
x: Jan Sunwai refers to public hearings associated with the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan in Rajasthan during the 1990s.

s: Which of the following pairs (citizen oversight tool – origin) is correctly matched?
o: Jan Sunwai – Public Affairs Centre, Bengaluru
Social audit – Gram Sabha audit of MGNREGA works
x: Social audit is the Gram Sabha's audit of scheme works; Citizen Report Cards come from the Public Affairs Centre and Jan Sunwai from MKSS.

s: In which year did the Indian rupee become convertible on the current account?
x: Current account convertibility came in 1994; capital account convertibility was never fully adopted.

s: Which of the following was NOT a part of the 1991 New Economic Policy?
o: Automatic approval for FDI in priority industries
Expansion of the list of industries reserved for the public sector
x: The 1991 policy cut licensing and shrank the public-sector reserved list; it never expanded State control.

s:
Consider the following statements about rupee convertibility:
1. The rupee was made convertible on the current account in 1994.
2. Full capital account convertibility was adopted as part of the 1991 LPG reforms.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Current account convertibility came in 1994; capital account convertibility was never fully adopted and was not part of LPG.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Chelliah (1991) dealt with tax reform; Narasimham with banking, Malhotra with insurance and Tarapore with capital account convertibility.

s: Which of the following committees dealt with insurance sector reform?
x: The Malhotra Committee (1993) dealt with insurance; Narasimham covered banking and Chelliah tax.

s: With which sector was the Narasimham Committee (1991) concerned?
x: The Narasimham Committee (1991, second in 1998) recommended banking sector reforms.

s: About how many tonnes of gold did India pledge with the Bank of England and UBS in 1991?
x: About 67 tonnes of gold were pledged with the Bank of England and UBS during the 1991 balance of payments crisis.

s: In the 1991 crisis, India approached the IMF for about how much assistance, with structural-adjustment conditions?
x: India approached the IMF for about $7 billion, which came with structural-adjustment conditions.

s: Which short-term reform measure targets the balance of payments, inflation and the fiscal deficit?
x: Stabilisation is short-term and corrects macroeconomic imbalances; structural adjustment is medium- or long-term and seeks efficiency and competitiveness.

s: Who were the Prime Minister and Finance Minister when the New Economic Policy of 1991 was announced?
o: Atal Bihari Vajpayee and Yashwant Sinha
P.V. Narasimha Rao and Dr. Manmohan Singh
x: The 1991 New Economic Policy was led politically by Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao and implemented under Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh.

s: Devaluation of the rupee in the 1991 reforms was which kind of measure?
x: Devaluation and deficit cuts were short-term stabilisation measures; delicensing was structural adjustment.

s: To about what level had India's foreign exchange reserves fallen in June 1991?
x: Reserves fell to $975 million in June 1991, about two weeks of imports; $7 billion was the IMF assistance sought.

s: Industrial delicensing in 1991 is classified as which kind of measure?
x: Structural adjustment (medium/long-term) covered delicensing, trade, financial, tax and PSU reforms; stabilisation targeted BoP, inflation and deficit.

s: On which date was the New Economic Policy (LPG) announced in India?
x: The NEP was announced on 24 July 1991 by PM P.V. Narasimha Rao's government with FM Manmohan Singh.

s: What was the trigger of India's 1991 balance of payments crisis?
x: NRI deposits flowed out, and forex reserves fell to about $975 million, enough for about two weeks of imports.

s: With which institutions did India pledge 67 tonnes of gold during the 1991 crisis?
o: Reserve Bank of India and State Bank of India
US Federal Reserve and Asian Development Bank
x: In 1991 India pledged 67 tonnes of gold with the Bank of England and UBS to raise foreign exchange.

s: Which of the following is true of globalisation in the LPG framework?
o: The precondition for liberalisation and privatisation
The outcome of liberalisation and privatisation
x: Globalisation, integration with the world economy, is the outcome of liberalisation and privatisation, not their precondition.

s: For which of the following was industrial licensing retained after the 1991 reforms?
o: Every industry employing more than 100 workers
Alcohol, cigarettes, hazardous chemicals and industrial explosives
x: Licensing was largely abolished but retained for alcohol, cigarettes, hazardous chemicals, industrial explosives, electronic aerospace and defence, and drugs.

s: In 1991, automatic approval was given for FDI up to what percentage in 34 priority industries?
x: The 1991 reforms allowed automatic approval for FDI up to 51 per cent in 34 priority industries.

s: In which year was FERA replaced by FEMA?
x: The Foreign Exchange Regulation Act framework was replaced by the Foreign Exchange Management Act in 1999.

s: Which committee examined capital account convertibility, which India has not fully adopted?
x: Capital account convertibility was never fully adopted; it was examined by the Tarapore Committees of 1997 and 2006.

s: By about how much was the rupee devalued in July 1991?
x: The rupee was devalued by about 20 per cent on 1 and 3 July 1991, leading to a market-determined rupee.

s: On which dates was the Indian rupee devalued in July 1991?
x: The rupee was devalued by about 20% in two steps, on 1 and 3 July 1991; the NEP itself came on 24 July 1991.

s: In LPG terminology, what does disinvestment mean?
o: Sale of part of a PSU's equity to the public
Government withdrawal from all economic activity
x: Disinvestment is the sale of part of a PSU's equity to the public; integration with the world economy is globalisation.

s: In which year were Navratna public sector undertakings given greater autonomy?
x: Nine PSUs were given Navratna status and greater autonomy in 1997. 1991 is the year of the reforms, not of the Navratna scheme.

s: What does the New Public Sector Enterprise Policy for Atmanirbhar Bharat (2021) favour?
x: The New PSE Policy, 2021 favours strategic disinvestment.

s: Above what level of private stake in a PSU does disinvestment transfer control to private hands?
x: Disinvestment is the sale of part of PSU equity; once the private stake goes above 51%, control passes to the private side.

s: Which subject did the Rangarajan Committee (1993) deal with?
x: The Rangarajan Committee (1993) dealt with PSU disinvestment; Narasimham dealt with banking and Malhotra with insurance.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about India's Industrial Policy Resolutions?
o: The 1948 Resolution adopted a mixed economy with four categories of industries
Under the 1956 Resolution, Schedule C industries were left to the private sector
Under the 1956 Resolution, Schedule A listed 17 industries for the public sector
Under the 1956 Resolution, Schedule B listed 12 industries reserved exclusively for the private sector
x: Schedule B's 12 industries were mixed (public and private); it was Schedule C that was left to the private sector.

s: Under which Industrial Policy Statement were District Industries Centres established?
x: The 1977 Industrial Policy Statement of the Janata Government emphasised small and cottage industries and set up District Industries Centres.

s: Which Industrial Policy Statement allowed MRTP firms 25 per cent expansion?
x: The 1980 Statement focused on technology upgrading, export orientation and backward areas, and allowed MRTP firms 25 per cent expansion.

s: Which of the following pairs about the 1991 Industrial Policy Statement is INCORRECTLY matched?
x: The 1991 Statement emphasised de-licensing, restructured MRTP and sought PSU autonomy through MoUs; it did not expand licensing.

s: In which year was the MRTP Act enacted?
x: The MRTP Act was enacted in 1969, relaxed in 1980 and restructured in 1991 before being replaced by the Competition Act, 2002.

s:
Consider the following statements about the MRTP Act:
1. It was relaxed in 1980.
2. In 1991, its asset limits and pre-entry curbs on expansion, mergers and acquisitions were abolished.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: the MRTP Act was relaxed in 1980, and in 1991 its asset limits and pre-entry curbs were abolished.

s: Which Act replaced the MRTP Act, 1969?
x: The MRTP Act was replaced by the Competition Act, 2002, administered by the CCI; FEMA replaced FERA.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about India's generations of economic reforms?
o: First-generation reforms (1991-2000) included industrial delicensing and tariff cuts
First-generation reforms were mainly concerned with factor markets such as labour, land and power
First-generation reforms introduced the automatic FDI route
Second-generation reforms addressed fiscal rules and PSU disinvestment
x: Factor markets (labour, land, power) belong to the second-generation reforms of the 2000s, not the first generation.

s: Which of the following was a prescription of the Washington Consensus?
o: Import licensing to protect domestic industry
Higher trade barriers on foreign investment
x: The Washington Consensus advocated trade and FDI liberalisation, privatisation and deregulation, along with fiscal discipline and tax reform.

s: With which economist and year is the term 'Washington Consensus' associated?
x: The Washington Consensus was formulated by John Williamson in 1989.

s: Reforms of factor markets such as labour, land and power belong to which generation of reforms?
x: Factor-market reforms (labour, land, power) are second-generation reforms of the 2000s, not first-generation.

s: Under first-generation reforms, India's peak tariffs were cut from about 125 per cent to about what level?
x: First-generation reforms (1991-2000) cut tariffs from about 125 per cent to about 30 per cent.

s: From which date did India's Foreign Trade Policy 2023 come into effect?
x: The Foreign Trade Policy 2023 was announced on 31 March 2023 and came into effect from 1 April 2023.

s: How does India's Foreign Trade Policy 2023 differ from the earlier EXIM/Foreign Trade Policies?
o: It has no fixed end date and is updated as needed
It was framed by the RBI
It abolished export promotion schemes for MSMEs
x: Earlier trade policies ran for five years; FTP 2023 has no end date and is revised whenever needed.

s: Which set contains only instruments of the enabler State?
o: State ownership, licensing and price controls
Industrial licensing, MRTP controls and public-sector reservation
Commanding heights, state ownership and production controls
x: PPPs, DBT, GeM and UMANG are instruments through which the State enables delivery by private or civil-society actors.

s: Which shift in the role of the State does Andhra Pradesh's Deepam-2 scheme illustrate?
x: By supporting BPL families through DBT for LPG cylinders, Deepam-2 shows a shift from the State as direct provider to the State as enabler.

s: After LPG, which role did the State increasingly play under the shift from Government to Governance?
o: An actor withdrawn completely from the economy
x: The post-reform State moved from direct provider to facilitator, regulator and catalyst; it did not withdraw completely.

s: After 1991, towards which role did the RBI's position in the banking sector move?
o: Body that ceased to regulate banks
x: Reforms made the RBI a facilitator, freeing bank decisions and enabling private and foreign banks, but it still regulates.

s: What is a State that sets rules and uses independent regulators to police markets called?
x: The regulatory state sets rules and polices markets through independent regulators; the provider state owns and runs production.

s: What shift did the 1991 reforms bring about in the Indian economy?
x: The LPG reforms under P.V. Narasimha Rao and Dr. Manmohan Singh shifted the economy from state-controlled to market-oriented.

s: SEBI is an example of which model of the State?
x: SEBI is an independent regulator of the regulatory State; PPP, DBT, GeM and UMANG mark the enabler State.

s: How many free LPG cylinders a year does Andhra Pradesh's Deepam-2 scheme give to BPL families?
x: Deepam-2 gives 3 free LPG cylinders a year to BPL families through DBT.

s: Abolition of asset limits under the MRTP Act removed curbs on which of the following?
o: Concentration, entry, expansion, mergers and acquisitions
x: Abolition of MRTP asset limits removed curbs on concentration, entry, expansion, mergers and acquisitions.

s: Defence production, earlier among the industries reserved for the public sector, was opened to the private sector in which year?
x: Defence production was opened to the private sector in 2001, leaving atomic energy and railway operations as the reserved areas in many lists. 1991 is when the reserved list was cut to 8 (defence still in it); 1997 is the Navratna year; 2015 is when the last SSI items were de-reserved.

s: Through which of the following were public sector enterprises given greater autonomy?
o: MoUs and Navratna or Maharatna status
Transfer of PSUs to local governments
x: PSEs received greater autonomy through Memoranda of Understanding and Navratna or Maharatna status.

s: The number of industries reserved for the public sector changed in which sequence?
x: The public-sector reservation list was reduced in phases from 17 industries under Schedule A in 1956 to 8 in 1991 and later to 3.

s: What was the target when disinvestment in India began in 1991-92?
x: Disinvestment began in 1991-92 with a target of Rs 2,500 crore, first to bridge the fiscal deficit.

s: Which industries are now reserved for the public sector?
x: The reserved list fell from 17 to 8 to 3 and now 2: atomic energy and railway operations; defence was opened in 2001.

s: In which year were the last items reserved for the small-scale sector de-reserved?
x: The last SSI-reserved items were de-reserved in 2015; defence was opened to private players in 2001.

s: By which date must LIC reach 10% minimum public shareholding as per the SEBI deadline?
x: SEBI has given LIC time till 16 May 2027 to reach 10% minimum public shareholding.

s: What does the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) regulate?
x: CERC regulates power tariffs and inter-state transmission; TRAI regulates telecom, IRDA insurance and SEBI the securities market.

s: Which of the following pairs about the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme is correctly matched?
x: The scheme is administered by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency and carbon trading under it is regulated by CERC, not SEBI.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Economic Survey 2025-26's observations on regulators?
o: It recommended relying mainly on retired bureaucrats to staff regulators
It noted that regulators exercise legislative, executive and judicial powers
It recommended balancing regulatory independence with accountability
It suggested statutory timelines for clearances, with penalties for delay
x: The Survey proposed dedicated regulatory careers for younger professionals instead of relying mainly on retired bureaucrats.

s: Which body did SEBI, set up under the SEBI Act in 1992, replace?
x: SEBI (1992) replaced the Controller of Capital Issues as the securities regulator.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: TRAI was set up in 1997; SEBI dates from 1992, CERC from 1998, IRDA from 1999 and PNGRB from 2006.

s: Which sector does the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB), set up in 2006, regulate?
x: PNGRB (2006) regulates petroleum products and gas pipelines; TRAI handles telecom and CERC power.

s: What is the title of the Economic Survey 2025-26 chapter that called for dedicated regulatory careers for younger professionals?
x: Chapter 3 of the Economic Survey 2025-26, 'Refining the Regulatory Touch', asked for regulatory careers for younger professionals instead of retired bureaucrats.

s: Which of the following was cited as an aspect of government failure that justified the 1991 reforms?
o: Complete autonomy of PSUs from political influence
x: Mounting losses, low efficiency, labour problems, project delays and lack of autonomy of PSUs were cited as government failure.

s: The intellectual basis for the argument that government failure necessitated the 1991 reforms was provided by which of the following?
o: Embedded autonomy theory associated with Peter Evans
Developmental-state theory associated with Chalmers Johnson
Public choice theory associated with James Buchanan
Flailing-state theory associated with Lant Pritchett
x: Public choice theory, associated here with James Buchanan, supplied the intellectual basis for the government-failure critique of the pre-1991 system.

s:
Which of the following are market failures that justified the planning-era role of the State?
1. Public goods
2. Externalities
3. Information asymmetry
x: Public goods, externalities, monopoly and information asymmetry are all market failures that justified an active planning-era State.

s: Which of the following was identified as a criticism of the economic reforms?
o: Expansion of public investment in agricultural infrastructure
Fall in public investment in agricultural infrastructure
Rise in revenue available for welfare due to tax incentives
x: Critics pointed to falling public investment in agricultural infrastructure, welfare revenue lost to tax incentives and curtailed social-sector spending.

s: What was a major criticism of disinvestment?
o: PSU assets were undervalued and proceeds plugged revenue gaps
Proceeds were used only for social infrastructure
It prevented all private participation in PSUs
x: Critics held that PSU assets were undervalued and proceeds filled revenue gaps instead of developing PSUs or social infrastructure.

s: What is the meaning of “Minimum Government, Maximum Governance”?
o: A leaner State that does less itself but governs better through rules, technology and accountability
A State that directly provides every service through public enterprises
A State that withdraws from all regulation and public accountability
A State that replaces all public institutions with private companies
x: The expression refers to a leaner State that performs fewer activities directly but governs more effectively through rules, technology and accountability.

s: Which of the following is NOT an instrument associated with e-governance for reducing discretion and middlemen?
x: Aadhaar, DBT and GeM are e-governance instruments that can reduce discretion and middlemen. Navratna status concerns autonomy for public sector enterprises, not e-governance.

s: Since which year has the slogan 'Minimum Government, Maximum Governance' been used?
x: The slogan dates from 2014: a leaner State governing better through rules, technology and accountability.

s: Besides the IMF and the World Bank, with which institution was the Washington Consensus package associated?
x: The Washington Consensus was associated with the IMF, World Bank and US Treasury; the WTO is not part of it.

s: In the Washington Consensus, market-determined interest rates fall under which prescription?
x: Market-determined interest rates are part of financial liberalisation; a competitive exchange rate is the exchange-rate prescription.

s: Interest-rate deregulation in India's 1991 reform package followed the recommendations of which committee?
x: Interest rates were deregulated on the Narasimham Committee line; tax cuts followed the Chelliah Committee.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Washington Consensus:
1. It was set out by John Williamson in 1989.
2. Market-determined interest rates and a competitive exchange rate are one single prescription.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: market-determined interest rates and a competitive exchange rate are separate prescriptions.

s: In which year did India move to a market-determined exchange rate?
x: After the 1991 devaluation, India moved to a market-determined exchange rate in 1993.

s: Who used the term “flailing state” in 2009 in relation to India?
x: Lant Pritchett used the concept of the “flailing state” in 2009 in relation to India.

s: Who is associated with the idea of 'embedded autonomy', a bureaucracy insulated from capture yet tied to business?
x: Peter Evans gave the idea of embedded autonomy (1995); Chalmers Johnson gave the developmental state.

s: Who among the following is associated with the 'developmental state' model, based on Japan's MITI (1982)?
x: Chalmers Johnson described the developmental state (1982, Japan MITI); Pritchett coined 'flailing state'.
